blocks.text: An image is an ordered stack of read-only layers; RUN, COPY and ADD each add one, while ENV, CMD, LABEL and similar only change the config. overlay2 merges the layers (lowerdir) with a per-container writable layer (upperdir) into the view the process sees.

blocks.src: generate: Stacked diagram: read-only image layers as lowerdir, a thin writable upperdir, and the merged view; a read falls through to the topmost layer containing the file; a write copies the whole file up first
blocks.alt: overlay2: reads fall through, writes copy up.
blocks.caption: overlay2: reads fall through, writes copy up.

items: Read: served from the topmost layer containing the file.
First write to an existing file: copy-up of the entire file into upperdir (appending to a 1 GB file copies 1 GB).
Delete: a whiteout in the upper layer; the bytes remain below.
Shared layers are stored and transferred once across images.

blocks.code:
# BAD: the cache stays in the first layer
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y build-essential
RUN rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
# GOOD: create and delete in the same layer
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends build-essential \
 && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

blocks.text: A secret copied in one layer and deleted in the next is still extractable. Databases on the writable layer are slow (copy-up) and die with the container; use volumes.

Q: "Why doesn't deleting files in a later RUN shrink the image?" A: "Layers are immutable; the delete only adds a whiteout on top. The bytes stay in the earlier layer, so cleanup must happen in the same RUN that created the files."

items: Image size = sum of all layers.
Copy-on-write copies whole files on first modification.
Clean up in the same layer; later deletes don't help.
